t: Unit and Measurement Normalizer: a plain-language overview
title: Unit and Measurement Normalizer: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Unit and Measurement Normalizer does and why archives need it. A unit and measurement normalizer makes all measurements speak the same language. '5 miles', '8 kilometers', and '26,400 feet' all become the same number of meters, so they can be compared, sorted, and analyzed together. It reads the number, reads the unit, checks they make sense together, and converts.
demo:
# Unit and Measurement Normalizer - runnable demo (JAH-ATK178-000001)
import re
RANK = 1
SIG = False
ITEMS = ['5 mi', '8 km', '26400 ft', '12 m']
TABLE = {"km": 1000.0, "m": 1.0, "cm": 0.01, "mm": 0.001, "mi": 1609.34, "ft": 0.3048,
         "kg": 1.0, "g": 0.001, "lb": 0.453592, "s": 1.0, "min": 60.0, "h": 3600.0}
DIM = {"km": "L", "m": "L", "cm": "L", "mm": "L", "mi": "L", "ft": "L",
       "kg": "M", "g": "M", "lb": "M", "s": "T", "min": "T", "h": "T"}
for item in ITEMS:
    m = re.match(r"\s*([\d.]+)\s*([a-zA-Z]+)\s*$", item)
    if not m or m.group(2) not in TABLE:
        print("%-12s -> UNPARSEABLE/UNKNOWN UNIT" % item); continue
    v, u = float(m.group(1)), m.group(2)
    si = {"L": "m", "M": "kg", "T": "s"}[DIM[u]]
    print("%-12s -> %.4g %s  [dimension %s]" % (item, v*TABLE[u], si, DIM[u]))
if RANK >= 3:
    print("units known:", len(TABLE))
if SIG:
    print("Signature lineage stamp: JAH-SIG-UNT-" + "JAH-ATK178-000001")
print("record:", "JAH-ATK178-000001", "OK")

t: How the Unit and Measurement Normalizer works
title: How the Unit and Measurement Normalizer works
description: Overview: what the Unit and Measurement Normalizer does and why archives need it. Real normalizers parse measurements with regular expressions that split values from unit symbols, look each unit up in a conversion table (Pint, UDUNITS, or the SI brochure's definitions), and verify dimensional consistency — lengths convert to lengths, never to seconds. Compound units ('m/s', 'kg·m²') are decomposed into base dimensions, uncertainties propagate through conversions, and the original text is always preserved alongside the normalized value. Temperature scales get special handling because Celsius-to-Kelvin is an offset, not a ratio.

t: How the Unit and Measurement Normalizer works: the deep tour
title: How the Unit and Measurement Normalizer works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Unit and Measurement Normalizer does and why archives need it. Real normalizers parse measurements with regular expressions that split values from unit symbols, look each unit up in a conversion table (Pint, UDUNITS, or the SI brochure's definitions), and verify dimensional consistency — lengths convert to lengths, never to seconds. Compound units ('m/s', 'kg·m²') are decomposed into base dimensions, uncertainties propagate through conversions, and the original text is always preserved alongside the normalized value. Temperature scales get special handling because Celsius-to-Kelvin is an offset, not a ratio. Advanced systems detect implicit units from instrument context, resolve ambiguous symbols ('m' as meter vs minute) by dimensional context, and flag physically impossible values (a human height of 300 meters). Quality is measured by conversion accuracy on annotated measurement corpora and by dimensional-error catch rate. The limits are archaic units with disputed definitions and dimensionless quantities masquerading as measurements — both are normalized with their uncertainty and provenance recorded rather than silently 'fixed'.

description: Production: how the Unit and Measurement Normalizer runs at archive scale and plugs into the extraction pipeline. Real normalizers parse measurements with regular expressions that split values from unit symbols, look each unit up in a conversion table (Pint, UDUNITS, or the SI brochure's definitions), and verify dimensional consistency — lengths convert to lengths, never to seconds. Compound units ('m/s', 'kg·m²') are decomposed into base dimensions, uncertainties propagate through conversions, and the original text is always preserved alongside the normalized value. Advanced systems detect implicit units from instrument context, resolve ambiguous symbols ('m' as meter vs minute) by dimensional context, and flag physically impossible values (a human height of 300 meters). Quality is measured by conversion accuracy on annotated measurement corpora and by dimensional-error catch rate. The limits are archaic units with disputed definitions and dimensionless quantities masquerading as measurements — both are normalized with their uncertainty and provenance recorded rather than silently 'fixed'.
